content.publication_text: If $3p7q8$ is divisible by $44$, list all possible pairs of values for $p$ and $q$.

content.text:
$1$. $44$ is $4 \times 11$, and $4$ and $11$ share no factor, so the number must pass both tests.
$2$. For $4$ the last two digits $q8$ must be a multiple of $4$: $08$, $28$, $48$, $68$ and $88$ all are, so $q$ is even.
$3$. For $11$: $8 - q + 7 - p + 3 = 18 - (p + q)$ must be $0$ or a multiple of $11$, so $p + q$ is $7$ or $18$.
$4$. $p + q = 18$ needs $p = q = 9$, which is odd; $p + q = 7$ with $q$ even gives $(7$, $0)$, $(5$, $2)$, $(3$, $4)$, $(1$, $6)$.
Answer: ($p$, $q) = (7$, $0)$, $(5$, $2)$, $(3$, $4)$, $(1$, $6)$

overview.goal: The student decides when two divisibility rules can be combined and produces a machine checked counterexample when they cannot.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A claim written across the top of a working surface with a strip of numbers beneath it, the way a statement on the board sits above the numbers used to test it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A claim says that passing two divisibility tests gives the third, and a single number from the strip is allowed to end it.
overview.concept: Passing the tests for two divisors gives divisibility by their product only when the two divisors share no common factor. 2 and 4 share the factor 2, so passing both says less than it looks and 12 breaks the claim. 2 and 3 share nothing, so passing both really does give 6.
overview.purpose: The student decides when two divisibility rules can be combined and produces a machine checked counterexample when they cannot.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Claim top, strip centre, verdict card beneath. Contrast panel to the right on a wide frame and below the verdicts on a 390 px frame. Every strip number keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show whether the combination holds while a prediction is still open, and never accept a counterexample without verifying it. An unverified counterexample teaches that naming a number is testing it.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. If a and b share a factor, then a number can satisfy both while carrying that shared factor only once, which is not enough for the product. 12 has 2 twice, which satisfies 2 and 4, but 8 needs three twos. When a and b share nothing, satisfying both forces every prime of a and every prime of b to be present to full strength, and those requirements do not overlap, so the product follows. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with the claim for 2 and 4 written across the top, an untouched strip and no verdict anywhere, and ask the class to answer yes or no out loud and give a reason. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the pair 2 and 4 with nothing tested. Never test a number before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Pull 12 out of the strip and test it, so the three verdict chips fill left to right as two passes and one failure. Point at the third chip. Target the number 12 against the pair 2 and 4, and read all three verdicts from the tool's own chips. Call 3. Put the pair 2 and 3 beside it in the contrast panel and let the two highest common factors appear last, then ask what is different about the pairs. Targets the contrast pair 2 and 3 and the two highest common factor badges, both read from the tool rather than from this plan.

One verified counterexample ends a combination claim

observationsAndConclusions.why: It carries the shared prime only as often as the larger divisor needs, not as often as the product needs
observationsAndConclusions.observe: One number lifts out of the strip passing the first two tests and failing the third
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: One verified counterexample ends a combination claim outright, however many numbers passed before it

observationsAndConclusions.why: Passing both tests forces every prime of each divisor to full strength, and the two demands do not overlap
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Sweeping a pair that shares no factor across the whole strip turns up no counterexample at all
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An empty search is explained by the condition, so nobody has to keep searching

observationsAndConclusions.why: The shared factor is what gets counted twice in the product while the number supplies it only once
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The highest common factor printed beside each pair is more than 1 for the failing claim and exactly 1 for the working one
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The highest common factor of the pair is what decides whether the combination is legitimate

media.description: Combined Divisibility Trap. Pass two tests. Must you pass the product test? Hunt the trap. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the combination claim from its own divisors, shows the question, then reveals the counterexample or the confirmation and the reason together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the claim on screen and the verdict HIDDEN, and asks whether dividing by 2 and by 4 must give 8. Beat 2 pulls 12 off the strip, which divides by 2 and by 4 and not by 8, so the claim falls to one number. Beat 3 puts the working pair beside it, 2 and 3 giving 6, and asks what is different about the two pairs. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setClaim, testNumber, showContrast and say.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own claim. Find a counterexample, verify a true combination, or state the condition on the two divisors. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the highest common factor that settles it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student sets any pair of divisors, tests any number on the strip, and types any rule about when combining works. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

scenes.subGoal: A divisor of 1 is the boundary case of the coprime condition, and the claim holds there.
scenes.onScreen: The scene built from this checkpoint's own numbers, the question set cleanly above it, and nothing else. One worked item: the claim, the strip, the question, then the counterexample or the confirmation and the reason together.
scenes.animation: Test: the three verdict chips fill left to right over 200 ms, so a counterexample is recognised as a pattern of two passes and a fail.
scenes.interaction: The agent lands this step with gotoStep, the animation plays, the class predicts out loud, then the agent calls reveal(). The board then fills one line per step.
scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: Every whole number divides by 1, so the first test rules nothing out. | Passing both tests is then the same as passing the test for 5. | A counterexample would have to pass the test for 5 and fail it at the same time. | The highest common factor of 1 and 5 is 1, so the claim holds. Answer: No: the highest common factor of 1 and 5 is 1, so the combination holds

scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: An empty search over one range is evidence and not yet a reason. | The highest common factor of 4 and 9 is 1. | So a number passing both carries two factors of 2 and two factors of 3 with no overlap. | 4 times 9 is 36, so every such number is a multiple of 36 and no counterexample exists anywhere. Answer: That none exists at all, because the highest common factor of 4 and 9 is 1

concept.notation: A combination claim is written as divisible by a and by b means divisible by a times b. The highest common factor of a and b is written as their HCF.
concept.statement: Passing the tests for two divisors gives divisibility by their product only when the two divisors share no common factor. 2 and 4 share the factor 2, so passing both says less than it looks and 12 breaks the claim. 2 and 3 share nothing, so passing both really does give 6.
misconceptions: Divisibility rules combined by multiplying the divisors regardless of shared factors.
A working pair taken as evidence that all pairs combine.
concept.why_it_is_true: If a and b share a factor, then a number can satisfy both while carrying that shared factor only once, which is not enough for the product. 12 has 2 twice, which satisfies 2 and 4, but 8 needs three twos. When a and b share nothing, satisfying both forces every prime of a and every prime of b to be present to full strength, and those requirements do not overlap, so the product follows.
worked_numbers: 12 divides by 2 and by 4 but not by 8, so the claim for 2 and 4 fails.
20 does the same, so counterexamples are not rare.
12 divides by 2 and by 3 and by 6, and every number that passes 2 and 3 passes 6, because their HCF is 1.

Asking whether a total that shares among 3 and among 5 must share among 15

textbook: The printed statement that a number divisible by both 9 and 4 must be divisible by 36

The printed counterexample of a number divisible by 4 and by 6 and not by 24
The printed use of prime factorisation to explain why checking 3 and 8 settles 24 while checking 4 and 6 does not

answer_key.worked: Two rules combine to their product exactly when the divisors share no common factor. 2 and 4 share a factor, so 12 breaks the claim; 2 and 3 share none, so 6 follows.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn claim: whether the combination holds, the highest common factor of the pair, and whether a submitted counterexample genuinely breaks it.
answer_key.precision: Counterexamples are found by search over a bounded range rather than from a hard coded list, so any valid number is accepted. Exact integer arithmetic throughout.
answer_key.ground_truth: hcf(a, b) = the Euclidean algorithm. combinationHolds(a, b) = hcf(a, b) is 1. counterexamples(a, b) = every n in the searched range divisible by a and by b but not by a times b.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.

steps: Every whole number divides by 1, so the first test rules nothing out.
Passing both tests is then the same as passing the test for 5.
A counterexample would have to pass the test for 5 and fail it at the same time.
The highest common factor of 1 and 5 is 1, so the claim holds.
items.answer: No: the highest common factor of 1 and 5 is 1, so the combination holds

steps: Every multiple of 9 is already a multiple of 3, so the first test adds nothing.
The number 9 passes both tests and fails the test for 27.
18 and 36 fail in exactly the same way.
Every multiple of 9 that is not a multiple of 27 is a counterexample.
items.answer: Very plentiful: 9, 18 and 36 all pass both tests and fail the test for 27

Passing the test for 3 puts one factor of 3 into it.
2 and 3 share no factor, so those two demands do not overlap.
For 2 and 4 the shared factor 2 is asked for twice, and one factor of 2 can serve both.
items.answer: Because 2 and 3 share no factor, while 2 and 4 share the factor 2
items.method: Explain why one pair combines and a similar looking pair does not

The highest common factor of 4 and 9 is 1.
So a number passing both carries two factors of 2 and two factors of 3 with no overlap.
4 times 9 is 36, so every such number is a multiple of 36 and no counterexample exists anywhere.
items.answer: That none exists at all, because the highest common factor of 4 and 9 is 1

That happens to be right, since 9 passes both tests and fails the test for 27.
Now take the pair 5 and 7, where both are odd, so the rule predicts no combination.
5 and 7 share no common factor, so every number passing both carries a factor of 35.
The pair does combine, so the rule fails on a pair it was not built from.

animations: Test: the three verdict chips fill left to right over 200 ms, so a counterexample is recognised as a pattern of two passes and a fail.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the claim falls to ONE number in front of the class. The three chips fill left to right, pass, pass, fail, and the third chip contradicts the rule the student is silently applying, which is 'multiply the divisors'. Never announce that 12 is a counterexample; let the pattern be the announcement, and ask the class out loud, before the beat, whether passing 2 and 4 must give 8.

Beat 2 answers the question the counterexample raises: WHY was one number enough? The prime bricks show 12 carrying the factor 2 twice while 8 demands it three times, and the strip's rail fills with 25 more counterexamples up to 200, so this is a pattern and not a lucky number. Keep the HCF off the screen here, it has not been earned yet.

Beat 3 is where the deciding quantity finally arrives. The two claims sit on the SAME strip, so the difference cannot be blamed on the numbers tested, and only then do the two HCF badges appear: 2 for the pair that breaks, 1 for the pair that holds. Say 'shares no common factor apart from 1' beside 'HCF is 1', the words carry the meaning that the abbreviation only labels.

media.instructions_for_student: The claim at the top says that passing both divisibility tests gives the test for their product. Tap numbers on the strip: each one shows you three verdicts at once. A counterexample has to pass BOTH single tests and fail the test for the product, nothing else counts, and the tool checks the one you submit. Sweep the strip when you think there is nothing to find, and read the two lines it gives you: what was searched, and whether anything could have been there at all. In Free Play, change the pair of divisors and watch the highest common factor change with it.

topics.summary: To test for a number, test for factors that share no common factor and multiply to it: 2 and 3 for 6, 3 and 8 for 24. Factors that share a factor, like 4 and 6, only test for their LCM.

content.text:
More on Divisibility Shortcuts
How can we find out if a number is divisible by 6?
Will checking its divisibility by its factors 2 and 3 work? Use the shortcuts for 2 and 3 on these numbers and divide each number by 6 to verify: 38, 225, 186, 64.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if a number is even and its digit sum is a multiple of 3, must it be a multiple of 6?
2. A number divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by their LCM, and the LCM of 2 and 3 is 6.
3. So test the units digit for 2 and the digit sum for 3.

A number divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by their LCM, and the LCM of 2 and 3 is 6.

How about checking divisibility by 24? Will checking the divisibility by its factors, 4 and 6, work? Why or why not?
Determining divisibility by 24 by checking divisibility by 4 and by 6 does not work. For example, the number 12 is divisible by both 4 and 6, but not by 24.
To check for the divisibility by 24, we can instead check for the divisibility by 3 and divisibility by 8.

content.text:
$1$. $38$ is even, but $3 + 8 = 11$ is not a multiple of $3$, so $38$ fails the test for $3$.
$2$. $225$ has digit sum $9$, but it is odd, so it fails the test for $2$.
$3$. $186$ is even and $1 + 8 + 6 = 15$ is a multiple of $3$, so it passes both: $186 = 6 \times 31$.
$4$. $64$ is even, but $6 + 4 = 10$ is not a multiple of $3$.
Answer: Only $186$ is divisible by $6$

content.text: Use prime factorisation to explain why $12$ passes the tests for $4$ and $6$ but is not divisible by $24$, and why the tests for $3$ and $8$ never let such a number through.
content.question: Use prime factorisation to explain why 12 passes the tests for 4 and 6 but is not divisible by 24, and why the tests for 3 and 8 never let such a number through.

content.publication_text: Use prime factorisation to explain why $12$ passes the tests for $4$ and $6$ but is not divisible by $24$, and why the tests for $3$ and $8$ never let such a number through.

content.text:
$1$. $12$ is $2 \times 2 \times 3$: divisible by $4$, which is $2 \times 2$, and by $6$, which is $2 \times 3$.
$2$. $24$ is $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3$ and needs three $2s$, but $12$ has only two, because $4$ and $6$ share a $2$.
$3$. $8$ is $2 \times 2 \times 2$ and $3$ shares no factor with it, so a number passing both holds $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3$.
$4$. The LCM of $3$ and $8$ is $24$, while the LCM of $4$ and $6$ is only $12$.
Answer: $4$ and $6$ only test for $12$, their LCM; $3$ and $8$ test for $24$

content.text: If $48a23b$ is a multiple of $18$, list all possible pairs of values for $a$ and $b$.

content.text:
$1$. $18$ is $2 \times 9$, and $2$ and $9$ share no factor, so the number must pass both tests.
$2$. For $2$, $b$ must be even.
$3$. For $9$, $4 + 8 + a + 2 + 3 + b = 17 + a + b$ must be a multiple of $9$, so $a + b$ is $1$ or $10$.
$4$. $a + b = 1$ with $b$ even gives $(1$, $0)$; $a + b = 10$ with $b$ even gives $(2$, $8)$, $(4$, $6)$, $(6$, $4)$, $(8$, $2)$.
Answer: ($a$, $b) = (1$, $0)$, $(2$, $8)$, $(4$, $6)$, $(6$, $4)$, $(8$, $2)$

content.text: Write five multiples of $36$ between $45000$ and $47000$. Share your approach with the class.

content.publication_text: Write five multiples of $36$ between $45000$ and $47000$. Share your approach with the class.

content.text:
$1$. $36$ is $4 \times 9$, and $4$ and $9$ share no factor, so a multiple of $36$ passes the tests for $4$ and $9$.
$2$. $45000 = 36 \times 1250$, so $45000$ is itself a multiple of $36$.
$3$. Keep adding $36$: $45036$, $45072$, $45108$, $45144$, $45180$.
$4$. Check $45108$: its last two digits $08$ make a multiple of $4$, and its digit sum $18$ is a multiple of $9$.
Answer: $45036$, $45072$, $45108$, $45144$, $45180$

content.text: Write a $6$-digit number that is divisible by $15$, such that when the digits are reversed, it is divisible by $6$.
content.question: Write a 6-digit number that is divisible by 15, such that when the digits are reversed, it is divisible by 6.
content.question_tex: Write a $6$-digit number that is divisible by $15$, such that when the digits are reversed, it is divisible by $6$.
content.publication_text: Write a $6$-digit number that is divisible by $15$, such that when the digits are reversed, it is divisible by $6$.

content.text:
$1$. Divisible by $15$ means divisible by $3$ and $5$; the reversed number must be divisible by $2$ and $3$.
$2$. The units digit must be $0$ or $5$, and it becomes the first digit when reversed, so it must be $5$.
$3$. The first digit becomes the units digit when reversed, so it must be even, say $2$.
$4$. Choose the middle digits so the digit sum is a multiple of $3$: $200025$ has digit sum $9$.
$5$. $200025$ ends in $5$ with digit sum $9$, and $520002$ is even with digit sum $9$.
Answer: For example $200025$ (reversed $520002$); any number starting with an even digit, ending in $5$, with digit sum a multiple of $3$ works

media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 5 (Checking Divisibility Quickly). Add the digits. Turn the dial. Find the pattern. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Digital Root Dial. Add the digits. Turn the dial. Find the pattern. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: The digital root is what is left when digits are added again and again, and it equals the remainder on division by 9 with 9 in place of 0. Adding a number moves the root forward round a dial of nine places by the root of that number, and multiples of 9 do not move it.
tool_config.title: Digital Root Dial
tool_config.screen: A dial with the numbers 1 to 9 round it and a pointer for the digital root. A number can be typed in and its digits folded step by step; a step button adds a chosen number, and the pointer jumps by that number's root. A trail records each stop.
feedback: A wrong landing place shows the root of the added number and the steps round the dial.
A number whose digits fold to 9 is marked as a multiple of 9, not as 0.
The remainder on division by 9 is shown beside the root after each card.
tool_config.done_when: All six cards are done with each landing place predicted before the step.

media.description: Adding the digits of a number again and again until one digit is left gives its digital root, and that digit is the remainder on division by nine. Two numbers show the idea, one with remainder two and one that is a multiple of nine. Keeko's doubt is that the digital root of four thousand five hundred eighty one is eighteen.

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step one, take four lakh eighty nine thousand seven hundred ten.
Four plus eight plus nine plus seven plus one plus zero is twenty nine.
<bookmark mark='again'/>Twenty nine has two digits, so we add again.
Two plus nine is eleven.
<bookmark mark='root'/>Eleven has two digits too.
One plus one is two, so the digital root is two.

marks.rem: remainder 2 is written beside the digital root 2

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step two, the digit sum leaves the same remainder as the number on division by nine.
Twenty nine is three nines and two more.
<bookmark mark='rem'/>The number leaves remainder two on division by nine, the same as its digital root.

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step three, take nine hundred ninety.
Nine plus nine plus zero is eighteen.
<bookmark mark='root'/>Eighteen has two digits, so we add again.
One plus eight is nine, and the digital root is nine.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>A root of nine means nothing is left over.
Nine times one hundred ten makes nine hundred ninety.

narration: <bookmark mark='k1'/>Kiko has one question to ask.

If it does not match, there is a mistake, so they add again.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.

topics.summary: The digital root is the single digit left after adding digits repeatedly. It equals the remainder on division by 9, except that multiples of 9 have digital root 9, so digital roots of consecutive numbers cycle through 1 to 9.

content.text:
Digital Roots
Take a number. Add its digits repeatedly till you get a single-digit number. This single-digit number is called the digital root of the number. For example, the digital root of the number 489710 will be 2 (4 + 8 + 9 + 7 + 1 + 0 = 29; 2 + 9 = 11; 1 + 1 = 2).
What property do you think this digital root will have? Recall that we did this while finding the divisibility shortcut for 9.
Aryabhata II's (c. 950 CE) work Mahāsiddhānta, mentions the method of computing the digital root of a number by repeatedly adding the digits till a single-digit number is obtained. This method is known to have been used to perform checks on calculations of arithmetic operations.

content.text:
1. Predict first: what single digit is left if you keep adding the digits of 489710?
2. Adding the digits keeps the remainder on division by 9, so the digital root is that remainder.
3. The one difference: a multiple of 9 has digital root 9, not 0.
4. Aryabhata II described this method over a thousand years ago to check calculations.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the digital roots of 489710 and 4581, and say what they tell you about division by 9.
1. 4 + 8 + 9 + 7 + 1 + 0 = 29. Then 2 + 9 = 11, and 1 + 1 = 2.
2. So 489710 has digital root 2 and leaves remainder 2 on division by 9.
3. 4 + 5 + 8 + 1 = 18. Then 1 + 8 = 9.
4. So 4581 has digital root 9 and is a multiple of 9: 4581 = 9 × 509.
Answer: 489710 has digital root 2 (remainder 2); 4581 has digital root 9 (a multiple of 9)

1. Predict first: what are the digital roots of 25, 26, 27, ..., 36?
2. Each step of 1 raises the digital root by 1, and after 9 it starts again at 1.
3. Multiples of 3 add 3 each time, so their roots cycle 3, 6, 9; multiples of 6 cycle 6, 3, 9.
4. Multiples of 4 add 4 each time and pass through all nine roots before repeating.

content.text:
Worked example: Write the digital roots of the consecutive multiples of 4 from 4 to 36, and of the numbers 7, 13, 19, 25, 31, which are 1 more than multiples of 6.
1. 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36 have digital roots 4, 8, 3, 7, 2, 6, 1, 5, 9.
2. Each step adds 4 to the root, taking away 9 when it passes 9, so all nine roots appear before the cycle repeats.
3. 7, 13, 19, 25, 31 have digital roots 7, 4, 1, 7, 4.
4. Adding 6 is the same as taking away 3 from the root, so 6k + 1 cycles through 7, 4, 1.
Answer: Multiples of 4 cycle through all nine roots; numbers 1 more than multiples of 6 cycle 7, 4, 1

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students find the digital root of a number by adding its digits repeatedly, and connect it with the remainder on division by 9.
Students list the numbers between 600 and 700 with a given digital root by stepping through the range in nines.
Students write digital roots of consecutive numbers and of consecutive multiples of 3, 4 and 6, and explain the cycles they see.
Students solve a riddle about a number whose digits, digit count, digit sum and digital root all point to the largest odd single digit.
Students predict how digital roots change when a fixed number is added, find the digital root of an expression, and make conjectures linking digital roots with parity and remainders.

segments.summary: The digital root is the single digit left after adding digits repeatedly. It equals the remainder on division by 9, except that multiples of 9 have digital root 9, so digital roots of consecutive numbers cycle through 1 to 9.

content.text:
$1$. The tiniest odd digit is $1$, so every digit is $1$.
$2$. The largest odd single digit is $9$, so there are nine digits.
$3$. Nine ones have digit sum $9$ and digital root $9$.
Answer: $111111111$

content.text: The digital root of an $8$-digit number is $5$. What will be the digital root of $10$ more than that number?
content.question: The digital root of an 8-digit number is 5. What will be the digital root of 10 more than that number?
content.question_tex: The digital root of an $8$-digit number is $5$. What will be the digital root of $10$ more than that number?
content.publication_text: The digital root of an $8$-digit number is $5$. What will be the digital root of $10$ more than that number?

content.text:
$1$. $10$ is $9 + 1$, so adding $10$ adds $1$ to the remainder on division by $9$.
$2$. So the digital root goes up from $5$ to $6$.
$3$. Check with $10000004$: its digital root is $5$, and $10000014$ has digital root $6$.
Answer: $6$
steps: 10 is 9 + 1, so adding 10 adds 1 to the remainder on division by 9.

Check with 10000004: its digital root is 5, and 10000014 has digital root 6.

content.text: Write any number. Generate a sequence of numbers by repeatedly adding $11$. What would be the digital roots of this sequence of numbers? Share your observations.
content.question: Write any number. Generate a sequence of numbers by repeatedly adding 11. What would be the digital roots of this sequence of numbers? Share your observations.
content.question_tex: Write any number. Generate a sequence of numbers by repeatedly adding $11$. What would be the digital roots of this sequence of numbers? Share your observations.
content.publication_text: Write any number. Generate a sequence of numbers by repeatedly adding $11$. What would be the digital roots of this sequence of numbers? Share your observations.

content.text:
$1$. $11$ is $9 + 2$, so adding $11$ raises the digital root by $2$, taking away $9$ when it passes $9$.
$2$. Starting from $5$: $5$, $16$, $27$, $38$, $49$, $60$ have digital roots $5$, $7$, $9$, $2$, $4$, $6$.
$3$. The roots go up in twos and all nine roots appear before the pattern repeats.
Answer: The digital roots go up by $2$ each time (after $9$, start again), so all nine appear before repeating

content.text: What will be the digital root of the number $9a + 36b + 13$?
content.question: What will be the digital root of the number 9a + 36b + 13?
content.question_tex: What will be the digital root of the number $9a + 36b + 13$?
content.publication_text: What will be the digital root of the number $9a + 36b + 13$?

content.text:
$1$. $9a$ and $36b$ are multiples of $9$, so they leave no remainder on division by $9$.
$2$. So the number leaves the same remainder as $13$, and $1 + 3 = 4$.
$3$. Check with $a = 1$ and $b = 1$: $9 + 36 + 13 = 58$, and $5 + 8 = 13$, then $1 + 3 = 4$.
Answer: $4$

content.text: Make conjectures by examining if there are any patterns or relations between (i): the parity of a number and its digital root. (ii): the digital root of a number and the remainder obtained when the number is divided by $3$ or $9$.
content.question: Make conjectures by examining if there are any patterns or relations between (i) the parity of a number and its digital root. (ii) the digital root of a number and the remainder obtained when the number is divided by 3 or 9.
content.question_tex: Make conjectures by examining if there are any patterns or relations between (i): the parity of a number and its digital root. (ii): the digital root of a number and the remainder obtained when the number is divided by $3$ or $9$.
content.publication_text: Make conjectures by examining if there are any patterns or relations between (i): the parity of a number and its digital root. (ii): the digital root of a number and the remainder obtained when the number is divided by $3$ or $9$.

content.text:
$1$. (i): $10$ is even with digital root $1$, and $11$ is odd with digital root $2$; $12$ is even with root $3$.
$2$. So the parity of a number does not decide the parity of its digital root.
$3$. (ii): The digital root equals the remainder on division by $9$, except that a root of $9$ means remainder $0$.
$4$. The remainder on division by $3$ is the remainder of the digital root on division by $3$: $3$, $6$ and $9$ give $0$.
Answer: (i): No fixed link between parity and digital root (ii): The digital root is the remainder on division by $9$ ($9$ for remainder $0$), and its remainder on division by $3$ is the number's remainder on division by $3$

media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 5 (Digits in Disguise). Every letter hides a digit. Solve it column by column. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.

The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's grid, the solution, and the column that decided it.

overview.goal: The student uses place value and carrying constraints to deduce digits rather than testing all options, and explains one deduction in words.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A vertical addition written with letters in place of digits, a carry row above it and a tray of digits beneath, the way a puzzle is set out in a notebook. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: Every letter hides a digit, and the class is asked to fix one of them without trying a single assignment.
overview.concept: A cryptarithm is solved by constraints, not by trying every assignment. Two rules always hold: different letters take different digits, and a leading letter is never 0. Working column by column from the units, each column plus its incoming carry fixes what is possible, and in an addition of two numbers the carry out of any column can only be 0 or 1.
overview.purpose: The student uses place value and carrying constraints to deduce digits rather than testing all options, and explains one deduction in words.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Addition centred in the main panel with the carry row above and the digit tray below. Notes panel to the right on a wide frame and collapsed to an expandable strip beneath on a 390 px frame. Every letter cell keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not name a wrong letter, and do not reveal any digit while a prediction is still open. Naming the letter would replace the deduction with a correction.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The largest sum in a column of two digits plus an incoming carry is 9 plus 9 plus 1, which is 19, so the carry out is at most 1. That single fact fixes a leading letter created by a carry to be 1 immediately. Each column is then a small equation in the letters it contains plus a known carry, and solving those in order is far shorter than searching, which is why the tool reports the failing column rather than the failing letter. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A leading letter is never 0, because that would change the length of the number. Breaks: Ignoring carries, and allowing a leading zero. Breaks: Trial and error without using the constraints, so feedback is used in place of deduction. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): A puzzle without a unique solution is flagged, never graded as though one answer were the only one. Breaks: Assuming every digit puzzle has exactly one answer.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the puzzle and every letter empty, and asks which digit a named letter definitely cannot be. Beat 2 places a digit that follows from the ones column and that column turns green, with the carry shown above the next one. Beat 3 uses the leading letter and the fact that a carry cannot exceed one to fix it, so a deduction rather than a search does the work. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeDigit, showCarry, checkColumns and say. No drag: the agent places a digit by naming the letter.
whatYouLearned: Different letters hold different digits and a leading letter is never 0
A carry in an addition of two numbers is only ever 0 or 1
Columns are solved in order from the units, which is shorter than any search
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the puzzle with every letter empty, no column green and the carry row blank, and ask the class to name out loud one digit a stated letter definitely cannot be, with a reason. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the units column of the opening puzzle. Never place a digit before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Place the digit that follows from the units column and let that column turn green with its carry travelling to the next. Point at the carry as it moves. Target the units column and its outgoing carry, and read every value from the tool's own grid. Call 3. Ask why the leading letter can only be 1, then place it and let the column verdicts follow. Targets the leading letter and the digit 1. Never name a wrong letter; name the failing column instead and let the class find the letter.

hunts: UNITS FIRST: solve a puzzle using only the units column and the carry, and see how far that alone gets you.
BREAK A RULE: try a leading zero and a repeated digit on purpose, and read the two refusals.
CARRY HUNT: build a puzzle whose total has one more digit than the addends, and say what its leading letter must be.
EXPLAIN ONE: solve any puzzle, then write the single deduction you are surest of.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each column is a small equation in its own letters plus a known carry, so it can be judged on its own
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A column turns green as soon as its letters and its incoming carry agree, before any other column is touched
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Working column by column from the units is far shorter than searching, because each column removes options for the rest

observationsAndConclusions.why: The carry out of two digits plus an incoming carry is at most 1, since 9 plus 9 plus 1 is 19
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A total with one more digit than the numbers added fixes its leading letter immediately
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A single bound on the carry settles a letter with no trial and no error at all

observationsAndConclusions.why: Different letters stand for different digits, and a leading zero would change how many digits the number has
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A repeated digit and a leading zero both spring back with the rule named
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The two standing rules are what make each placement informative rather than a guess

media.description: Digit Puzzle Solver. Every letter hides a digit. Solve it column by column. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the puzzle from its own letters, shows the question, then reveals the deduction chain, the filled grid and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the puzzle and every letter empty, and asks which digit a named letter definitely cannot be. Beat 2 places a digit that follows from the ones column and that column turns green, with the carry shown above the next one. Beat 3 uses the leading letter and the fact that a carry cannot exceed one to fix it, so a deduction rather than a search does the work. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeDigit, showCarry, checkColumns and say. No drag: the agent places a digit by naming the letter.

Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's grid, the solution and the column that decided it.

scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: The largest a column of two digits plus an incoming carry can reach is 9 plus 9 plus 1. | 9 plus 9 is 18. | 18 plus 1 is 19. | So the carry out of any column is 0 or 1. | A new leading column holds only that carry, so its letter is 1. Answer: Because the carry out of a column is at most 1, so the new leading digit can only be 1

scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Each letter stands for one digit, the same digit everywhere it appears. A carry is written above the column it enters and is always 0 or 1 in an addition of two numbers.
concept.statement: A cryptarithm is solved by constraints, not by trying every assignment. Two rules always hold: different letters take different digits, and a leading letter is never 0. Working column by column from the units, each column plus its incoming carry fixes what is possible, and in an addition of two numbers the carry out of any column can only be 0 or 1.
misconceptions: Trial and error without using the constraints, so every assignment is tested in turn.
Ignoring carries, and allowing a leading zero.
concept.why_it_is_true: The largest sum in a column of two digits plus an incoming carry is 9 plus 9 plus 1, which is 19, so the carry out is at most 1. That single fact fixes a leading letter created by a carry to be 1 immediately. Each column is then a small equation in the letters it contains plus a known carry, and solving those in order is far shorter than searching, which is why the tool reports the failing column rather than the failing letter.
worked_numbers: A leading letter produced by a carry must be 1, because a carry cannot exceed one.
In the units column, the sum of the two letters ends in the answer's units digit, which rules out most digits at once.
Two different letters can never take the same digit, so each placement removes a digit from every other letter.

textbook: The printed cryptarithms in which one two digit number is added to another and each letter stands for one digit

answer_key.worked: The leading letter must be 1 because a carry cannot exceed one, and each column then fixes its letters in turn.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn puzzle: which columns are currently consistent, and whether the full assignment solves the addition.
answer_key.precision: Solved by constraint propagation at load time to confirm uniqueness. The carry chain is checked explicitly column by column and never inferred from the final total.
answer_key.ground_truth: columnConsistent(i, assignment) = the column sum plus its incoming carry matches the answer digit and produces the stated outgoing carry. solution = the letter to digit map found by constraint propagation. isUnique = whether propagation found exactly one.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

constraints: Different letters always hold different digits, and no leading digit may be zero. Both are enforced at placement with the reason stated.
The tool never says which letter is wrong, only which column fails, so deduction rather than correction is required.
Column checking handles the carry chain explicitly, so a column is judged on its own terms and not by whether the final total came out.
Every puzzle is solved by constraint propagation at load time to confirm uniqueness, and a non unique puzzle is flagged rather than served silently.
The notes panel records ruled out digits and is never used by the checker, so the student's reasoning aids stay theirs.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

steps: The largest a column of two digits plus an incoming carry can reach is 9 plus 9 plus 1.
9 plus 9 is 18.
18 plus 1 is 19.
So the carry out of any column is 0 or 1.
A new leading column holds only that carry, so its letter is 1.
items.answer: Because the carry out of a column is at most 1, so the new leading digit can only be 1
items.method: Bound the carry out of a column and fix a leading letter by deduction

visual_behaviour.scene: A vertical addition with letters in place of digits, a carry row above the columns, and a digit tray beneath. A consistent column takes the primary accent behind it; an unjudged column stays neutral. The notes panel lists each letter with the digits ruled out against it.

animations: Column green: a column that becomes consistent fills behind its digits over 180 ms, so progress is per column rather than per letter.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 is the definition, shown rather than asserted. The puzzle is on screen with every letter empty, the two standing rules sit beside it, and the ghost of the same total drawn one column short is what says WHY a leading letter cannot be 0, the number would stop being a three digit number. Ask the class out loud which digit a named letter definitely cannot be, and commit their answer with predict(); never place a digit before that.

Beat 2 is the whole justification in one picture, and it is the beat that breaks the commonest error on this topic. The worst possible column is drawn live, 9 and 9 with an incoming carry of 1, the total 19 forms, and only the 1 detaches and travels to the next column while the 9 stays. Say the qualifier every time: this is an addition of TWO numbers. Section 5.3 also prints ON + ON + ON and QR + QR + QR, where three addends push the carry to 2, and a class that carries an unqualified rule into that exercise is stuck.

Beat 3 spends the bound. The leading column of A B + C A = B B C holds nothing but the carry, so B is 1 by deduction and not by search; A and C then follow from the units and tens columns and all three columns turn green from the units end. Point at the carry as it travels. Read every number off the tool's own grid, from state.truth, and never from your own arithmetic.

content.text:
Let us now try solving some cryptarithms involving multiplication. (v) PQ × 8 = RS.
Guna says, "Oh, this means a 2-digit number multiplied by 8 should give another 2-digit number. I know that 10 × 8 = 80. But the units digits of 10 and 80 are the same, which we don't want. For the same reason PQ cannot be 11 as P and Q correspond to different digits. 12 × 8 = 96 fits all the conditions". Can PQ be 13? Think.
It is not possible because 13 × 8 = 104. For all 2-digit numbers greater than 12, the product with 8 is a 3-digit number.

(vii) Here is one more: BYE × 6 = RAY.
Anshu says, "Since the product is a 3-digit number, B can't be 2 or more. If B = 2, i.e., 2 hundreds, the product will be more than 1200. So, B = 1."
What can you say about 'Y'? What digits are possible/not possible?
"Y cannot be 7 or more because, if Y = 7, then 170 × 6 = 1020; but we want a 3-digit product. Also, Y will be even", Anshu explains.
We can solve cryptarithms using patterns, properties, and reasoning related to numbers and operations.

maths_rules: (i) UT × 3 = PUT: 3 × T ends in T, so T is 0 or 5; T = 5 gives carry 1 and 3 × U + 1 is odd, so it cannot end in U; T = 0 needs 3 × U to end in U, so U = 5 (U is not 0); 50 × 3 = 150, P = 1
(ii) AB × 5 = BC has two digits, so AB is at most 19 and A = 1; 5 × (10 + B) = 50 + 5B must have tens digit B; only B = 9 works, 19 × 5 = 95, C = 5

(iii) L2N × 2 = 2NP: the answer is under 300, so L2N is under 150 and L = 1; 2 × 2 + carry = N, so N = 4 (no carry, 2 × 4 = 8) or N = 5 (carry 1, 2 × 5 = 10); 124 × 2 = 248 (P = 8), 125 × 2 = 250 (P = 0)
(iv) XY × 4 = ZX has two digits, so XY is at most 24; 4 × Y is even and ends in X, so X = 2; 4 × Y ends in 2 for Y = 3 or 8; 28 is too big; 23 × 4 = 92, Z = 9

(v) PP × QQ = 11P × 11Q = 121 × P × Q; three digits needs P × Q at most 8; the last digit is P × Q and must be P, so Q = 1; P = 1 repeats Q; P = 5 or more gives 121 × P with the wrong first digit; 22 × 11 = 242, 33 × 11 = 363, 44 × 11 = 484

$1$. (i): Without a carry the tens would make $A = 3$, and then $B + 7$ could not end in $3$; so $B + 7$ carries $1$, $A$ is $2$ and $B$ is $5$: $25 + 37 = 62$.
$2$. (ii): $ON \times 3$ has only two digits, so $O$ is $1$, $2$ or $3$, and $3 \times N$ ends in $O$.
$3$. $O = 1$ needs $N = 7$: $17 \times 3 = 51$. $O = 2$ needs $N = 4$: $24 \times 3 = 72$. $O = 3$ needs $N = 1$: $31 \times 3 = 93$.
$4$. (iii): $3 \times R$ ends in $R$, so $R$ is $0$ or $5$; $R = 0$ would force $Q = 0$ too, so $R = 5$ with a carry of $1$, and $3 \times Q + 1$ ends in $5$, so $Q = 8$: $85 \times 3 = 255$.
Answer: (i): $25 + 37 = 62$; (ii): three solutions: $17$, $24$ or $31$, giving $51$, $72$ or $93$; (iii): $85 + 85 + 85 = 255$

content.text:
$1$. (i): $3 \times T$ ends in $T$, so $T$ is $0$ or $5$; $T = 5$ fails because $3 \times U + 1$ cannot end in $U$, and $T = 0$ gives $50 \times 3 = 150$.
$2$. (ii): $AB \times 5$ has two digits, so $AB$ is at most $19$, and $A$ is $1$; $19 \times 5 = 95$.
$3$. (iii): $2 \times N$ ends in $P$ and $2 \times 2$ plus the carry gives $N$, so $N$ is $4$ or $5$: $124 \times 2 = 248$ and $125 \times 2 = 250$.
$4$. (iv): $XY \times 4$ has two digits, so $X$ is $1$ or $2$, and $4 \times Y$ ends in $X$, so $X$ is $2$; $23 \times 4 = 92$.
$5$. (v): $PP \times QQ$ is $P \times Q \times 121$, and a $3$-digit product needs $P \times Q$ to be at most $8$.
$6$. The units digit of the product is then $P \times Q$ itself, and it must be $P$, so $Q = 1$: $22 \times 11 = 242$, $33 \times 11 = 363$, $44 \times 11 = 484$.
$7$. (vi): $KKK$ divided by $6$ must be a $2$-digit number ending in $K$: $222$, $444$, $666$ and $888$ give $37$, $74$, $111$ and $148$, and only $74$ ends in $4$; $74 \times 6 = 444$.
Answer: (i): $50 \times 3 = 150$; (ii): $19 \times 5 = 95$; (iii): $124 \times 2 = 248$ or $125 \times 2 = 250$; (iv): $23 \times 4 = 92$; (v): $22 \times 11 = 242$, $33 \times 11 = 363$ or $44 \times 11 = 484$; (vi): $74 \times 6 = 444$

content.text:
$1$. (i): $GGG$ is $111 \times G$, which is $3 \times 37 \times G$, so $EF \times E$ must contain the factor $37$.

topics.summary: Properties of divisibility, the shortcuts for 3, 9 and 11 and why they work, and proving patterns with algebra, pictures, examples and counterexamples.

content.text:
We explored and learnt various properties of divisibility:
If a is divisible by b, then all multiples of a are divisible by b. If a is divisible by b, then a is divisible by all the factors of b. If a divides m and a divides n, then a divides m + n and m − n. If a is divisible by b and is also divisible by c, then a is divisible by the LCM of b and c.
We learnt shortcuts to check divisibility by 3, 9 and 11, and why they work.
Through all this we were exposed to the power of mathematical thinking and reasoning, using algebra, visualisation, examples and counterexamples.

content.text:
1. Our opening question is settled: signs between four numbers always give results of one parity, because switching a sign changes the result by twice a number.
2. Divisibility passes to multiples, to factors, to sums and differences, and to the LCM of two divisors, but not always to their product.
3. Place values leave remainder 1 on division by 9 and 3, and alternately one more and one less on division by 11. Still open for you: find a shortcut of your own for 99.

content.text:
Navakankari, also known as Sālu Mane Āṭa, Chār-Pār, or Navkakrī, is a traditional Indian board game that is the same as 'Nine Men's Morris' or 'Mills' in the West. It is a strategy game for two players where the goal is to form lines of three pawns to eliminate the opponent's pawns or block their movement.
Gameplay. 1. Each player starts with 9 pawns. The players take turns in placing their pawns on the marked intersections. An intersection can have at most one pawn. 2. Once all the pawns are placed, the players take turns to move one of their pawns to adjacent empty intersections to form lines of three. The line can be horizontal or vertical. 3. Once a player makes a line with their pawns they can remove any one of the opponent's pawns as long as it is not a part of one of their lines.
A player wins if the opponent has less than 3 pawns or is unable to make a move.

content.text:
Worked example: Your partner has two pawns in a line with the third point empty, and it is your turn to place a pawn. What should you do, and why?
1. If you leave the empty point, your partner completes a line of three next turn.
2. A completed line lets your partner remove one of your pawns.
3. Placing your pawn on the empty point blocks the line.
Answer: Place your pawn on the empty point to block the line of three

modules.module_summary: Cryptarithms with addition and multiplication are solved by reasoning about digits, carries and sizes, followed by the chapter summary and the game of Navakankari.

objectives.objective_text: Students write numbers as sums of two or more consecutive numbers, find numbers that can be written in more than one way, and notice which numbers cannot be written at all.
Students list all eight ways of placing plus and minus signs between four consecutive numbers, evaluate each one, and notice that every result is even.
Students take any four numbers, show with algebra that switching one sign changes the value by twice a number, and conclude that all eight expressions have the same parity.
Students use the rules for the parity of sums and differences, and the token model, to explain why the signed expressions share one parity for any count of numbers, not only four.
Students flip signs between four numbers to predict parity, and describe runs of consecutive numbers with a single letter-number.
Students use the parity rules for sums, differences, products and powers to tell whether an arithmetic expression is even without working it out.
Students show that an expression such as 4m + 2q is even for all integers by finding a factor of 2, and show that x² + 2 is not always even with one example and one non-example.
Students sort the remaining expressions into always even and not always even, with examples and non-examples, and write expressions of their own that are always even.
Students sort even numbers by their remainder on division by 4 into multiples of 4 (4p) and numbers that are 2 more than a multiple of 4 (4p + 2), using dot grids of four columns.
Students explain with algebra and dot grids that two multiples of 4, or two numbers of the form 4p + 2, always add to a multiple of 4.
Students explain the mixed case of a multiple of 4 plus a number of the form 4q + 2, and extend the idea to sums of two multiples of 3.
Students show with algebra and dot rows that a number dividing two numbers divides their sum and difference, and use a counterexample to show the converse is only sometimes true.
Students explain why multiples of a multiple of 7 stay multiples of 7, why a multiple of 12 is divisible by every factor of 12, and when a multiple of 7 is divisible by another multiple of 7.
Students decide that a number divisible by 9 and by 4 is divisible by 36, but a number divisible by 6 and by 4 need not be divisible by 24, and state the LCM rule.
Students show with parity and with algebra that an odd number added to an even number can never give a multiple of 6.
Students sort statements about multiples, products and consecutive numbers into always, sometimes and never true, proving each verdict with algebra, an example or a counterexample.
Students list numbers that leave remainder 3 on division by 5, choose the expressions 5k + 3 and 5k − 2 that capture all of them, and reject the others with a counterexample.
Students find the remainder of a sum or difference from the remainders of the two numbers, writing each number as a multiple plus its remainder.
Students list numbers that meet two remainder conditions, notice that they repeat every LCM of the divisors, and write one expression for all of them.
Students write expressions for numbers with given remainders, test claims about them, and solve remainder puzzles.
Students write a number in the general form 1000d + 100c + 10b + a and explain why it is divisible by 10 exactly when its units digit is 0.
Students explain with place values why the units digit alone decides divisibility by 5 and by 2.
Students use the rule bench to shade place values that are multiples of 4 or 8 and explain why the last two or three digits decide divisibility by 4 and 8.
Students explain why any number made only of the digits 9 and 0 is divisible by 9, and why the units digit alone cannot test for 9.
Students show that every place value is one more than a multiple of 9, and add the digits to find the remainder of a number on division by 9.
Students judge four statements linking a number's divisibility by 9 with its digit sum, and see that all four follow from the if and only if rule.
Students explain that every place value also leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, and use the digit sum to test divisibility by 3.
Students split numbers into nines and ones to test divisibility by 9, find multiples of 9 with given properties, and explain why shuffling the digits keeps a multiple of 9.
Students find that place values alternate between one more and one less than a multiple of 11, and use this to decide whether 462 is divisible by 11.
Students add the digits in the places that are one more and those that are one less than a multiple of 11, and use the difference to find the remainder on division by 11.
Students place alternating signs before the digits starting from the units digit, evaluate the expression, and compare this procedure with the excess and shortfall method.
Students use the shortcut for testing divisibility by 11 to find remainders, and find missing digits that make a number divisible by 44.
Students check divisibility by 6 by testing for 2 and for 3, and verify by dividing.
Students explain with prime factorisation why testing for 3 and 8 checks divisibility by 24, while testing for 4 and 6 does not.
Students fill a divisibility table quickly, find missing digits that make a number a multiple of 18, and build numbers that pass two tests at once.
Students find the digital root of a number by adding its digits repeatedly, and connect it with the remainder on division by 9.
Students list the numbers between 600 and 700 with a given digital root by stepping through the range in nines.
Students write digital roots of consecutive numbers and of consecutive multiples of 3, 4 and 6, and explain the cycles they see.
Students solve a riddle about a number whose digits, digit count, digit sum and digital root all point to the largest odd single digit.
Students predict how digital roots change when a fixed number is added, find the digital root of an expression, and make conjectures linking digital roots with parity and remainders.
Students state the rules of a cryptarithm and solve an addition cryptarithm column by column, using the units digit and the carry.
Students use the number of digits in a product to limit the possible values in a multiplication cryptarithm.
Students match the multiplier H with the units digit of GH to pick the one solution of the cryptarithm GH × H = 9K from a list of options.
Students solve a three digit multiplication cryptarithm by bounding the hundreds digit, then the tens digit, and then the units digit.
Students solve addition and multiplication cryptarithms in the puzzle solver, using units digits, carries and the size of the product, and find every solution when there is more than one.
Students restate the properties of divisibility, the shortcuts for 3, 9 and 11 with their reasons, and the role of algebra, pictures, examples and counterexamples in proving patterns.

chapter_approach.intro: Number Play is about noticing a pattern and then proving that it must always happen. Each idea starts with a few numbers to try, a guess about what always happens, and then a reason using algebra, a dot picture or place value. Examples show a statement is true for those numbers; a single counterexample shows a claim is false.

points.text: Students try a pattern on a few numbers first, say what they think always happens, and only then write the letter-number or dot-grid reason that makes it certain.
points.title: Try, guess, then prove

points.text: Statements about divisibility are sorted by finding a proof (always), an example and a counterexample (sometimes), or a reason it can never hold (never).
points.title: Always, sometimes or never

points.text: Every divisibility shortcut is explained by the remainders that place values leave, so the shortcut for 9, 3 or 11 is understood and not just remembered.
points.title: Shortcuts with reasons

points.text: Ten tools, each used once: flipping signs between four numbers, dot grids of even numbers, testing a claim, remainder rows, a place-value rule bench, breaking a number into nines and ones, excess and shortfall for 11, a two-test trap for combined divisibility, a digital root dial, and a digit puzzle solver. The other ideas are taught without a tool because the reasoning itself is the move.
points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
